unit_label: ABFM Module D unit 2 (courseware unit 20): start-up finance

facts.statement: Start-up concept and the Start-up India initiative (courseware): a start-up is a business that is just getting started, created by one or more owners to provide a good or service for which they see a market; start-ups typically have high costs and little income and so seek funding from venture capitalists and other sources. They are described as companies or projects undertaken to seek, develop and validate a scalable business model, with high uncertainty and a high failure rate, but a minority become successful and influential. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) runs Start-up India, which includes an online hub and a recognition process; the Start-up India Action Plan of January 2016 set out recommendations in three categories: financial assistance and incentives, industry-academia collaboration, and simplification and handholding. Statistics on the number of recognised start-ups, unicorns and funding are narrative and not taught.

Benefits under the Start-up Plan (courseware, principles): tax incentives, government funding support, exemptions, priority treatment in public procurement, self-certification of compliance with some labour and environmental laws, relaxed inspection rules, fast-track exit when winding up (the insolvency law treats eligible start-ups as fast-track firms with a shorter winding-up period), rebates on patent and trademark filing fees, faster patent examination with facilitator support, and incubators (institutions that help entrepreneurs build businesses by providing capital, technological and laboratory resources, networking, mentoring and advice). Specific percentages, periods and amounts are not taught.

Definition of a start-up in India (courseware, elements only): an entity is a start-up if it is within a limit of years from incorporation or registration, if its turnover has not exceeded a limit in any financial year, if it is a private limited company, registered partnership firm or limited liability partnership, and if it works towards innovation, development, deployment or commercialisation of products, processes or services driven by technology or intellectual property, or is a scalable business with high employment or wealth generation potential; an entity formed by splitting up or reconstruction of an existing business is not a start-up. The courseware gives an initial definition and an expanded definition with different limits; the numerical limits are not taught.

Challenges and state policy (courseware): the main challenges listed are failure to plan appropriately, unrealistic expectations, knowledge and skills gaps, time management and productivity, lack of leadership, fierce competition, lack of demand and ineffective marketing, winning customer trust, hiring suitable candidates, partnership decision making, financial management, securing funding and cyber security. A state start-up policy provides funding, mentorship and market access, and incentives to key stakeholders such as incubators and higher education institutions, to encourage a start-up ecosystem; the courseware states that most states and union territories have their own policy.

Pitch presentation (courseware): a pitch presentation is a slide presentation used by an entrepreneur to showcase the business and give investors the reasons to invest; it came into use in the late 1990s during the dotcom boom. It should be clear and concise, emphasise the most significant aspects rather than every detail, answer the main questions an investor would have, be flexible according to the type of venture and address investor concerns. Contents to prepare: the problem statement, the solution, the business model, the technology used, business and commercial activity, the competitive environment, the team composition, predictions and significant events, the present status and timelines for execution, and an executive summary with a call for action.

Programmes and competitions for start-ups (courseware, types only): the courseware lists many government programmes, which can be grouped by purpose: grants to incubators (incubator challenge programmes under the Atal Innovation Mission), outreach to smaller cities and districts (the Start-up India Yatra), procurement support (an exemption from earnest money deposit and prior experience conditions for recognised start-ups in public procurement; a dedicated section on the government e-marketplace to let start-ups sell to government buyers), awards and rankings (national start-up awards; a states start-up ranking based on seven reform areas such as access to markets, support for incubation, institutions, innovation, funding, capacity building and mentoring), showcases and networking, women-focused programmes, sector grand challenges (animal husbandry, health, textiles, water quality, renewable energy, single-use plastics, mining), innovation zones in urban local bodies, research parks, and international bridges. The names, amounts, dates and statistics are not taught.

Tax and regulatory reliefs (courseware, purposes only): the courseware describes an exemption from tax on share issue premium above fair value on self-declaration, taxation of ESOPs as a perquisite with deferral of tax for eligible start-ups, a deduction of profit for a block of years for eligible start-ups, capital gains relief for individuals who invest in the equity of an eligible start-up, conditions for carry-forward of losses, and relaxation of the deposit rules for convertible notes taken by a start-up. The purposes are to ease cash needs in the early years, encourage investment and reduce the tax burden on employee stock options; the sections, percentages and periods are not taught.

Types of start-up financing (courseware): debt financing is borrowing money from a lender with interest within a set period, with no influence on the company, but the firm may need collateral; sources are banks, non-banking financial institutions and government loan programmes. Equity financing is selling shares of the company in exchange for capital: there is no obligation to repay the principal and no collateral is needed, but ownership is shared and investors often get a say in decisions; sources are incubators and accelerators, angel investors, venture capitalists, crowdfunding and friends and family. A grant is an incentive, usually financial, given by one organisation to another to promote a goal; it needs no payback, is often paid in stages with each stage depending on the previous one, and gives the grantor no return; sources are central or state governments, corporate challenges and private programmes.

Stages of start-up funding (courseware): at the idea stage the money needed is small and mostly informal; bootstrapping means growing only from the founders own resources and profits, with no obligation to repay or dilute control; friends and family are common, and a prize in a pitching competition may be enough. At the seed stage the company runs field trials, tests the product with a few clients, brings on mentors and builds a formal team; sources include incubators (offering space, utilities, advice and sometimes grants, debt or equity), seed fund schemes, angel investors (private individuals who invest in high-potential firms for a share of ownership, often through angel networks) and crowdfunding (many people each giving a small amount). At Series A, money is raised to build the user base, extend products and enter new geographies; venture capital funds (pools of money managed by professionals for companies with rapid growth, usually in exchange for ownership and with mentoring) are common, and with a market presence the firm can raise loans from banks and non-banking finance companies, or venture debt, which does not dilute equity. At the scaling stage larger venture funds with bigger ticket sizes are approached once the market response is validated. Exit options: another company buying the whole business or a part, an initial public offering (laborious, usually for firms with a record of earnings), sale of shares to other venture or private equity investors, or buy-back by founders.

Process of raising funds and what investors look for (courseware): the stages are determining whether money is needed, assessing the need for funding, assessing investment readiness, preparing the pitch deck, investor targeting, due diligence by an interested investor, and a term sheet. The company should plan by milestones with timetables and estimate costs over a period, including prototypes, research and manufacturing. Investors look, in order of importance, at the objective and problem solved, the management and team, the market landscape, scalability and sustainability, customers and suppliers, the competitive analysis, sales and marketing, the financial assessment and the exit avenues.

Seed fund scheme principles (courseware): the aim of a seed fund for start-ups is to support proof of concept, prototype development, product trials, market entry and commercialisation, so that the start-up can reach a stage at which it can attract angel investors, venture capital or bank loans. Eligibility principles: the start-up is recognised, is young, has a marketable idea that uses technology and has not already received a large amount of funding from other schemes (the amounts and dates are not taught). The scheme works through selected incubators that choose start-ups by a selection committee, with an expert committee overseeing the scheme. The incubator uses funds only for the start-ups (not for building facilities), disburses in instalments against milestones, keeps the funds in a dedicated account, reports on use of funds and progress against indicators, and does not charge fees to the start-ups. Two uses: grants for validation of a prototype, proof of concept or product trials, and investment in convertible debentures, debt or debt-linked securities for market entry, expansion or commercialisation. Amounts and percentages are not taught.

Fund of Funds and credit guarantee (courseware, principles): a fund of funds for start-ups was set up to increase the capital available, stimulate private investment and expand the start-up ecosystem. It does not invest directly in start-ups: it commits capital to SEBI-registered alternative investment funds (daughter funds), which in turn invest in start-ups; the selection and monitoring of the daughter funds is the duty of the managing development bank. A credit guarantee programme is meant to ease the access of early-stage entrepreneurs to loans by providing guarantee cover for the lender, reducing the collateral burden. Other sector programmes (for example for technology patents, renewable energy refinancing, biotechnology grants, defence technology funds and high-risk research) are designed around specific sectors and their eligibility conditions are not taught.

payload.title: What a start-up is and the Start-up India initiative
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **start-up** is a business in its **earliest stage**: one or more owners set it up to supply a good or service for which they see a market. It typically has **high costs and little income**, so it seeks **outside funding** (venture capital and other sources).

It is a company or project trying to **prove a business model that can scale**, amid **great uncertainty and a high rate of failure**; only a **minority** go on to become successful and influential.

**Start-up India** is run by the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)**. It includes an **online hub** and a **recognition process**. The **Action Plan of January 2016** grouped its recommendations under **three heads**: **simplification and handholding**, **funding support and incentives**, and **industry-academia partnership**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Statistics on recognised firms and unicorns in the courseware are narrative and are not taught.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT).

payload.title: Elements of the start-up definition
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A reconstructed business cannot take advantage of start-up benefits by relabelling itself.

self_check.prompt_text: Can a business formed by splitting up an existing company be treated as a start-up?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, such an entity is excluded from the definition.

payload.title: Benefits and support for start-ups
payload.core_explanation_md:
Start-ups recognised under the plan can receive:

- **Tax incentives** and **government funding support**.
- **Priority and relaxed conditions in public procurement**.
- **Self-certification** of compliance with some **labour and environmental laws** and **relaxed inspection**.
- **Fast-track exit**: eligible start-ups can be **wound up in a shorter period** under the insolvency law.
- **Rebates on patent and trademark filing fees** and **faster patent examination**.
- **Incubators**: institutions giving **capital, laboratories, technology, networking, mentoring and advice**.

**Percentages, periods and amounts are not taught.**
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The mix is meant to lower early-stage compliance cost and speed up a decision to close a failed venture.

self_check.prompt_text: What does an incubator provide to a young business?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Capital, technological and laboratory resources, networking, mentoring and advice.

payload.title: Challenges faced by start-ups and state start-up policy
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Main challenges:** **poor planning**, **unrealistic expectations**, **knowledge and skills gaps**, **time management**, **weak leadership**, **fierce competition and lack of demand**, **winning customer trust**, **hiring**, **partnership decisions**, **financial management**, **securing funding** and **cyber security**.

**State start-up policy:** a state policy gives **funding, mentorship and market access**, and **incentives to incubators and higher education institutions**, so that a **local ecosystem** develops. Most states and union territories have one.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Many failures come from weak planning and finance rather than from the idea itself.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two challenges that start-ups face.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example securing funding and fierce competition (any two from the list).

payload.title: The pitch presentation
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **pitch** is a **short slide presentation** that shows the business and gives investors **reasons to invest**. It became common in the **late 1990s dotcom boom**.

**It should be** **clear and concise**, stress the **most important points** rather than every detail, **answer the investor main questions**, be **flexible** to the type of venture and **address investor concerns**.

**Contents:** **problem statement**, **solution**, **business model**, **technology**, **business and commercial activity**, **competitive environment**, **team**, **forecasts and key milestones**, **current status and timelines**, **executive summary and call to action**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Investors back the team and the problem first, so these appear early in a pitch.

self_check.prompt_text: Name four items that a pitch should cover.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example the problem, the solution, the business model and the team.

payload.title: Kinds of government support programmes
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware lists many programmes; they fall into **types**:

| Type | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Incubator grant challenges** | Fund and improve **incubators** |
| **Outreach programmes** | Reach **smaller cities and districts** |
| **Procurement support** | **Relax tender conditions**; a **marketplace section** for start-ups to sell to government |
| **Awards and rankings** | **Recognise start-ups** and **rank states** (access to markets, incubation, institutions, innovation, funding, capacity building, mentoring) |
| **Sector grand challenges** | **Solve problems in a sector**: health, water, energy, textiles, plastics, mining and others |
| **Women-focused programmes** | Training, platform and **funding links** for women entrepreneurs |
| **Innovation zones, research parks** | Local **civic problems** and **research capacity** |
| **International bridges** | **Cross-border** collaboration with other countries |

**Names, amounts, dates and statistics are not taught.**
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Programmes change often, so the types and purposes are more useful than the names.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the purpose of a states start-up ranking?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To assess and compare how well states support the start-up ecosystem and to encourage reform.

payload.title: Tax and regulatory reliefs for start-ups (purposes)
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware describes reliefs of these kinds:

- Relief from **tax on the issue of shares above fair value** for eligible start-ups.
- **ESOP taxation** with **deferral** for eligible start-ups, easing the **cash burden** on employees.
- A **deduction for a block of years** for eligible start-ups.
- **Capital gains relief** for individuals who **reinvest in start-up equity**.
- **Conditions** for **carrying forward losses**.
- **Relaxed deposit rules** for **convertible notes** taken by a start-up.

**Purposes:** **ease cash needs in the early years**, **encourage investment** and **reduce the tax burden of option plans**. **Sections, rates and periods are not taught** because they have changed or may have changed.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Always check the provision in force at the time before relying on any relief.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do start-ups receive tax relief on ESOPs?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To ease the cash burden on employees who would otherwise pay tax before they can sell their shares.

payload.core_explanation_md:
| Stage | Typical sources |
| --- | --- |
| **Idea** | **Bootstrapping** (own resources and profits: **no dilution, no repayment**), **friends and family**, **competition prizes** |
| **Seed** | **Incubators**, **seed fund schemes**, **angel investors** (often through networks), **crowdfunding** |
| **Series A** | **Venture capital** (professionally managed pools for rapid-growth firms, with **mentoring**), **bank and NBFC loans**, **venture debt** (**no dilution of equity**) |

payload.title: Raising funds: process and what investors weigh
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Stages of the process:**

1. Decide **whether money is needed**.
2. **Assess the need** for funding.
3. Assess **investment readiness**.
4. Prepare the **pitch deck**.
5. **Target investors**.
6. **Due diligence** by an interested investor.
7. **Term sheet**.

Plan by **milestones with timetables** and estimate **costs over a period**, including **prototypes, research and manufacturing**.

**Investors weigh, in order:** **the objective and the problem solved**, **the management team**, **the market landscape**, **whether the business can scale and last**, **customers and suppliers**, **the competition**, **sales and marketing**, **the financials**, **exit routes**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Finance comes eighth in the list: investors first want a real problem and a capable team.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two things do investors rank first when judging a start-up?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The objective and problem it solves, and the management and team.

payload.title: Principles of a seed fund scheme
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Aim:** support **proof of concept, prototype development, product trials, market entry and commercialisation**, so the firm can later attract **angels, venture capital or bank loans**.

**Start-up eligibility (principles):** **recognised**, **young**, a **marketable technology-using idea**, and **not already heavily funded** by other schemes.

**Machinery:** **selected incubators** choose start-ups through a **selection committee**; an **expert committee** oversees the scheme.

**Controls:** funds go **only to start-ups** (not to build facilities), are paid **in instalments against milestones**, are held in a **dedicated account**, are **reported** against indicators, and **no fees** are charged to start-ups.

**Two uses:** **grants** for **validation** (prototype, proof of concept, trials); **investment** in **convertible debentures, debt or debt-linked securities** for **market entry or commercialisation**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Milestone-linked instalments limit the loss if a venture fails early.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are seed funds paid in instalments against milestones?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It keeps funds tied to progress and limits the loss if the venture fails.

payload.title: Fund of funds and credit guarantee
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Fund of funds (FoF):** set up to **increase capital for start-ups**, **stimulate private investment** and **expand the ecosystem**.

- It does **not invest directly** in start-ups.
- It commits capital to **SEBI-registered alternative investment funds (AIFs), the daughter funds**, which then **invest in start-ups**.
- The **managing development bank** **selects and monitors** the daughter funds.

**Credit guarantee:** a **guarantee for the lender** that makes it **easier for early-stage entrepreneurs to borrow** by **reducing the collateral burden**.

**Sector programmes** (patents, renewable refinancing, biotechnology grants, defence technology, high-risk research) have **specific eligibility** that is **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Using AIFs spreads the investment decisions to professional managers.

self_check.prompt_text: How does a fund of funds reach start-ups?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Indirectly, by investing in alternative investment funds that invest in start-ups.

payload.title: Equity round arithmetic: ownership, valuation and dilution
payload.core_explanation_md:
Selling equity means **giving a share of ownership for capital**. Standard arithmetic:

- **Post-money value = pre-money value + investment.**
- **Investor stake = investment / post-money value.**
- **Price per share = pre-money value / shares before the round**; **new shares = investment / price per share.**
- **Founder stake after a round = stake before x (1 - stake sold).** Repeated rounds **multiply** the retention factors.
- **Runway (months) = cash / monthly net burn**, where **net burn = expenses - revenue**.

Debt avoids dilution but needs **interest and repayment** and sometimes **collateral**.

assumptions: All new shares are issued at the round price
No other securities are issued in the round
common_errors: Dividing by the pre-money value instead of post-money value
Adding the percentages of successive rounds instead of multiplying retention

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A higher pre-money value lets founders give up less ownership for the same amount raised.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the investor stake in an equity round calculated?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The investment divided by the post-money value.

unresolved: This courseware unit is largely a catalogue of Indian government start-up programmes, schemes and statistics dated about 2021 and 2022 (recognition counts, fund sizes, grant amounts, eligibility conditions, competitions and challenges, research parks, international bridges). They are time-bound, were not checked against any primary source and are likely to have changed before the 30 June 2026 cut-off. They are not taught or tested as facts; only the types of support and their purposes are taught.

The courseware definition of a start-up (age and turnover limits for the initial and the expanded definition, recognition criteria) is held back: the figures are given as at the courseware date, a later notification may have changed them, and no primary source was retrieved. Only the elements of the definition (age limit, turnover limit, innovation or scalability, no splitting up or reconstruction of an existing business, recognition by the industry promotion department) are taught.

The courseware tax and regulatory reliefs (tax treatment of share issues above fair market value on self-declaration, ESOP taxation and deferral, a deduction for eligible start-ups, capital gains relief for reinvestment, loss carry-forward conditions, deposit-rule relaxation for convertible notes, the insolvency fast-track period) cite sections, percentages and periods that have changed or may have changed since the courseware date (in particular the angel-tax provision). No primary source was retrieved and none of these is taught or tested; only the purposes of such reliefs are mentioned.

The courseware statements about the Start-up India Seed Fund Scheme (amounts, number of instalments, percentages, committee membership, time limits) and the Fund of Funds (corpus, amounts committed) are scheme specifics that are not taught or tested; only the structure and principles are taught.

The ownership, valuation and dilution arithmetic in the numerical items (pre-money, post-money, stake after a round, price per share, convertible note discount, runway, burn) is standard finance arithmetic applied to the courseware principle that equity financing means selling shares for capital; the courseware does not itself use the terms pre-money or post-money.
